title: GROUP BY, HAVING, FILTER (WHERE ...)
summary: GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group, and aggregates summarize each group; WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. FILTER (WHERE ...) restricts the input of one aggregate, so several conditional counts come out of a single pass.

examples.title: One row per group, what count(*) counts, and WHERE vs HAVING

annotations.note: count(*) counts rows, count(duration_ms) only non-NULL values. avg skips NULLs too and divides by what it kept: export averages 900 over its one timed run, not 450 over two. avg of an integer column returns numeric, so search's 77.5 rounds to 78 instead of truncating.
WHERE removes rows before any group exists. export has no failed run, so it never becomes a group. An aggregate here is an error (SQLSTATE 42803): there is nothing to aggregate yet.

HAVING runs on the finished groups, so it can test aggregates: auth has one failure and is dropped. It can't use the output name failures, because the SELECT list is computed after it; repeat the expression.
Aggregates without GROUP BY treat all input as one group, and one group gives one row even when it is empty: count is 0, sum is NULL.
Add GROUP BY and the same empty input makes no groups at all: SELECT 0. A report that needs a row for every suite has to start from a list of suites and LEFT JOIN the runs (example 3).
A suite has several statuses, and PostgreSQL refuses to pick one. Group by status too, count it with FILTER (next example), or, if any value really will do, say so with any_value(status) (PG 16).

examples.title: FILTER for side-by-side counts, its CASE equivalent, and ratio traps

annotations.note: Each FILTER restricts the input of its own aggregate only. Unlike WHERE, it doesn't remove rows from the other columns or groups: export stays, with failed = 0. One scan produces the whole pivot.

The pre-9.4 spelling, still needed on databases without FILTER. It depends on an easy-to-miss detail: count(CASE ... END) works because a CASE without ELSE yields NULL, which count skips. Add ELSE 0 and it counts every row.
count returns bigint, and bigint / bigint is integer division: 2 / 3 is 0. No error, no warning, a column of zeros.
100.0 is numeric, so the whole expression is computed in numeric. round(value, digits) exists for numeric only; with a double precision value it fails to resolve.

export has no failed run, so the filtered sum sees no input: NULL, while count says 0. Every aggregate except count returns NULL on empty input; coalesce turns it into the 0 a chart or an API client expects.

examples.title: count(*) after a LEFT JOIN, grouping by the key, and Turkish İ/ı in lower()

annotations.note: REQ-EXPORT has no tests, so the LEFT JOIN gives it one row padded with NULLs. count(*) counts that row (1); count(t.id) counts matched tests (0). Count a column of the optional side that is never NULL in real rows, its primary key.

Grouping by the primary key makes every other column of requirements functionally dependent on it, so r.code may appear in SELECT without being grouped (PG 9.1). Group by the identity, not by a label that might repeat.

This database uses the builtin C.UTF-8 locale, where lower() applies Unicode simple case mapping: İ becomes i and I also becomes i. So 'DİYARBAKIR' turns into 'diyarbakir', which doesn't equal 'diyarbakır'. Iğdır splits the same way.

lower() follows the collation of its input. With tr-x-icu it applies Turkish rules (I to ı, İ to i), and each city becomes one group. The result carries the collation too, so ORDER BY sorts the keys in Turkish order.

use_cases: Reports and dashboards: runs per suite, failures per requirement, orders per customer per month
Pivot-style status columns (passed / failed / skipped) with FILTER, in one query instead of three or a client-side pivot
Data-quality checks with HAVING: duplicate e-mail addresses (HAVING count(*) > 1), requirements with fewer than two tests
Case-insensitive duplicate reports on names and cities, with the Turkish collation when the text is Turkish
strengths: The summary is computed next to the data: one row per group crosses the network, instead of every row being fetched and folded in Go or TS
FILTER puts several conditional aggregates into one scan and reads like the question; Java's Collectors need a filtering(...) downstream collector per column
Ambiguous selects are an error (SQLSTATE 42803) rather than an arbitrary pick, and any_value() (PG 16) makes 'any value will do' explicit
Grouping by a primary key lets you select every column of that table without listing them all in GROUP BY
weaknesses: NULL rules differ per aggregate: count gives 0 on empty input, sum, avg, min and max give NULL, and avg divides by the non-NULL count
Integer arithmetic on counts truncates silently: bigint / bigint is bigint
WHERE can't see aggregates and HAVING can't see SELECT aliases, so filtered totals repeat their expression or move to an outer query
Grouping compares text exactly; case-insensitive grouping needs an explicit normalization, and the correct one depends on the language

pitfalls.title: count(*) after a LEFT JOIN
pitfalls.detail: The NULL-padded row of an unmatched parent is still a row, so count(*) reports 1 where the answer is 0. Count a NOT NULL column of the optional side.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT r.code, count(*) FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id
pitfalls.good: SELECT r.code, count(t.id) FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.detail: count(*) is bigint, so passed / total is 0 for anything under 100%. Bring a numeric in first. A FILTERed denominator can be 0 (a suite with only skipped runs), so guard it with nullif or the query fails with division by zero.
pitfalls.good: round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE status <> 'skipped'), 0), 1)

pitfalls.title: An output name that shadows a column in GROUP BY
pitfalls.detail: GROUP BY accepts output column names, but when an input column has the same name, the input column wins (ORDER BY makes the opposite choice). This query groups by the raw city and returns 'diyarbakır' twice, with no error.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT lower(city) AS city, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city
pitfalls.good: SELECT lower(city) AS city_key, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY lower(city)

pitfalls.title: sum() of nothing is NULL
pitfalls.detail: A group whose FILTER matches no row, or a query with no input, gets NULL from sum, avg, min, max and array_agg; only count returns 0. Use coalesce where the consumer expects a number.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive grouping of Turkish text
pitfalls.detail: In the default C.UTF-8 collation lower() maps I to i, so 'DİYARBAKIR' and 'Diyarbakır' land in different groups. PG 18's casefold() doesn't fix it: in this database it leaves İ unchanged ('dİyarbakir'). Name the Turkish collation.

quiz.q: REQ-EXPORT has no test cases. What do count(*) and count(t.id) return for it in `requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id`?
quiz.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps REQ-EXPORT as one row with NULLs on the test side. count(*) counts that row; count(t.id) skips the NULL.

quiz.q: What does `SELECT count(*), sum(duration_ms) FROM test_runs WHERE false` return?
quiz.why: Without GROUP BY the input forms one group even when it is empty. count of nothing is 0; sum of nothing is NULL.

quiz.q: You want one row per suite with its number of failed runs, including suites with no failures. Which do you use?
options: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') ... GROUP BY suite
Either; they return the same rows
quiz.why: WHERE removes the rows before grouping, so a suite without failures has no rows left and disappears. FILTER only limits what that one aggregate sees.

quiz.q: A suite has 2 passed runs out of 3. What is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*)`?
quiz.why: Both counts are bigint, and integer division truncates toward zero. Multiply by 100.0 (numeric) first.

body:
## Concept

`GROUP BY` collapses all rows that share the grouping values into one output row, and
aggregate functions (`count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, ...) summarize the rows of each
group. Once a query groups, every expression in the SELECT list must be one of three
things: a grouping expression, an aggregate, or a column functionally dependent on a
grouped primary key. Anything else would need PostgreSQL to pick one value out of many,
and it refuses.

Two filters sit on either side of the grouping. `WHERE` decides which **rows** go in;
`HAVING` decides which **groups** come out, and can therefore test aggregates.
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` (PG 9.4) is a third, narrower one: it decides which rows a single
aggregate sees, so `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')` next to a plain `count(*)`
gives failures and totals from the same pass.

Most aggregates ignore NULL inputs. `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` counts non-NULL
values, and on empty input every aggregate except `count` returns NULL.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** pandas `df.groupby('suite').agg(...)` is the same idea.
  `itertools.groupby` only merges *adjacent* equal keys, so it needs sorted input;
  `GROUP BY` doesn't.
- **Java:** `runs.stream().collect(groupingBy(Run::suite, counting()))`. Each FILTER
  column would be its own `filtering(r -> ..., counting())` downstream collector.
- **JS:** `Object.groupBy(runs, r => r.suite)` (ES2024) builds the arrays and you reduce
  each one. SQL fuses grouping and reducing, and never materializes the groups' rows
  for you to look at.
- **Go:** a `map[string]*stats` filled in a loop, then sorted keys for stable output.
  The database does the same with a hash table or a sort, next to the data.
- In all of these, reading a field from "the group" without reducing it is something
  your code decides (the first element?). SQL makes you choose explicitly: group by it,
  aggregate it, or `any_value()` it.

## How it works

The clauses run in this logical order, which explains most of the rules above:

1. `FROM` and joins build the input rows.
2. `WHERE` keeps the rows for which its condition is true. No aggregates exist yet.
3. `GROUP BY` forms the groups; aggregates (with their `FILTER`s) are computed per group.
4. `HAVING` keeps the groups for which its condition is true.
5. The `SELECT` list is evaluated, output names come into existence.
6. `ORDER BY` sorts, and it may use those output names.

`HAVING` runs before step 5, so it can't refer to `failures`; it repeats `count(*)`.
PostgreSQL lets `GROUP BY` use output names as an extension, but an input column with
the same name takes precedence (see the pitfalls).

## Design notes

Prefer `FILTER` to `CASE` inside aggregates. It states the condition once, can't be
broken by a stray `ELSE 0`, and produces the same single-pass plan. Keep `CASE` for code
that must run on databases without `FILTER`.

Group by identities, not labels: `GROUP BY r.id` and select `r.code`, rather than
`GROUP BY r.code`, which silently merges two requirements if codes ever repeat.

Ratios are numeric work: bring in `100.0` or a cast before dividing, `nullif` any
denominator that can be zero, and round last.

Case-insensitive grouping is a normalization decision, and for Turkish text the default
one is wrong. `lower()` and `upper()` follow the collation of their input, so name it:
`lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`. Even that assumes Turkish typing: `IZMIR` typed on an
English keyboard becomes `ızmır` under Turkish rules. When the input is mixed, normalize
once on the way in instead of in every query.

files.examples/01_group_having.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.aggregation.group-by): one row per group; WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int              -- NULL: the run was skipped, nothing was timed
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'passed',  120), (2, 'auth',   'failed',  340),
  (3, 'auth',   'passed',  110), (4, 'export', 'skipped', NULL),
  (5, 'export', 'passed',  900), (6, 'search', 'failed',   75),
  (7, 'search', 'failed',   80), (8, 'search', 'skipped', NULL);

-- One output row per suite. count(*) counts rows; count(col) and avg skip NULLs.
SELECT suite,
       count(*)                AS runs,
       count(duration_ms)      AS timed,
       round(avg(duration_ms)) AS avg_ms
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- WHERE picks rows before grouping; HAVING picks groups after aggregation.
SELECT suite, count(*) AS failures
FROM test_runs
WHERE status = 'failed'
GROUP BY suite
HAVING count(*) >= 2
ORDER BY suite;

-- No GROUP BY: all input rows form one group, so even zero rows give one row.
SELECT count(*) AS runs, sum(duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM test_runs
WHERE suite = 'billing';

-- With GROUP BY, zero input rows make zero groups.
SELECT suite, count(*) AS runs
FROM test_runs
WHERE suite = 'billing'
GROUP BY suite;

-- Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. Which status per suite?
SELECT suite, status, count(*) FROM test_runs GROUP BY suite;
files.examples/02_filter.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int NOT NULL         -- 0 for skipped runs
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'passed',  120), (2, 'auth',   'failed',  340),
  (3, 'auth',   'passed',  110), (4, 'export', 'skipped',   0),
  (5, 'export', 'passed',  900), (6, 'search', 'failed',   75),
  (7, 'search', 'failed',   80), (8, 'search', 'skipped',   0);

-- One pass over the table, one row per suite, one column per status.
SELECT suite,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed')  AS passed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')  AS failed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'skipped') AS skipped,
       count(*)                                   AS total
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- The same counts the portable way: CASE inside the aggregate.
SELECT suite,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 'passed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS passed,
       count(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 END)      AS failed
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- count() returns bigint, and bigint / bigint truncates toward zero.
SELECT suite,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*) AS int_ratio,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'passed') / count(*), 1)
         AS pass_pct
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- A FILTER that matches no row: count says 0, sum says NULL.
SELECT suite,
       count(*)         FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_runs,
       sum(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_ms,
       coalesce(sum(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed'), 0)
         AS failed_ms_or_0
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;
